title: Tips on how to use Codex to generate quality VFX?
author: ZurkAtanis

comments.author: CalebKious
comments.body:
I’ve done a **lot** of VFX work with Codex/ImageGen for FateMMO—skill effects, spell animations, impact frames, projectiles, auras, etc.—and I’ve found that “memory” isn’t really the best solution to consistency.

What works much better is building a **reference-driven VFX pipeline**.

When I get an effect that is genuinely good, I preserve the actual output and use it as a visual reference for subsequent effects. Instead of saying “remember how we made that fire attack,” I’ll provide the successful sprite sheet/frame and say something closer to:

“Use this as the visual-quality/style reference. Preserve the same pixel density, perspective, edge treatment, lighting language and animation readability, but create an ice/lightning/etc. effect with this specific motion.”

I’ve also had much better results separating **designing the effect** from **generating the frames**.

Before generating anything, establish what the animation actually does:

anticipation → buildup → release → impact → dissipation

Then define what should change between frames. For example, a fireball shouldn’t just be eight independently generated pictures of fire. The silhouette should expand/contract logically, the core should travel consistently, trailing particles should follow the motion, and the impact needs a clear peak frame.

One of the biggest improvements for FateMMO was treating generated VFX as **source material rather than sacred final output**. If 6 frames are excellent and 2 are bad, don’t regenerate the entire thing and gamble again. Fix/regenerate those frames, composite pieces, remove artifacts, adjust timing, or manually touch them up.

I also keep different classes of effects visually related. Fire skills share certain characteristics, lightning has another language, healing another, legendary/rare effects another, etc. That gives the game’s VFX an identity instead of every ability looking like it came from a different AI prompt.

And use screenshots constantly.

I’ll put the VFX into the actual game, run it against the character/background/UI it’s supposed to coexist with, screenshot it, and feed that back to Codex:

“Effect is too large relative to the character.”

“Impact disappears against this environment.”

“Frames 4–5 don’t preserve the silhouette.”

“The brightest point needs to occur at impact.”

“Too much visual noise for a basic attack—reserve this intensity for higher-rarity abilities.”

That feedback loop is enormously more effective than endlessly tweaking the original prompt.

So my workflow is basically:

**good existing VFX → reference → define animation/motion → generate → put it in-game → screenshot → critique specific problems → selectively regenerate/edit → repeat.**

Also save your successful prompts/settings/reference sheets alongside the actual outputs. Don’t rely on model memory to reconstruct your art direction each time.

Once you have maybe 10–20 effects you’re really happy with, those should effectively become your game’s **VFX style guide**. Then Codex isn’t being asked “make me a cool effect” anymore; it’s being asked to produce something that belongs to an already-established visual language.

That distinction has made a huge difference for FateMMO.

replies.author: ZurkAtanis
replies.body:
Yeah makes sense, I'll start referencing the good stuff. It is surprising how often it just wants to do CSS even when I feel like I'm directing it away from that.

How do you save successful prompts? Is there a way in Codex that is reliable? Or do you just have separate files you can pull up?

Thank you!
